brief: Citadel Securities (Nohshad Shah) frames the global rise in yields via three drivers: the case for tighter policy (fiscal largesse, resilient labour markets, an energy shock atop above-target inflation), markets repricing real growth and the real rates the economy can absorb (risk-asset resilience under added tightening reads as not a recession signal, pulling 5y5y forward rates into the sell-off), and the AI-investment cycle becoming a large claim on capital markets beyond hyperscaler bonds (of roughly $500bn in AI-related debt issuance, hyperscalers account for under half; Apollo's $35bn private financing for Broadcom's AI platform shows other channels). That high-quality, long-dated supply is an alternative to sovereign duration and an added headwind for government bonds regardless of the growth/inflation outlook. America has more room to absorb this: 5-6% nominal growth cushions a ~3.5% average borrowing cost, though large enough primary deficits can still overwhelm favorable rate-growth dynamics. Europe has much less AI offset. France shows the asymmetry becoming a fiscal problem: 10y yields +130bp since end-2025 add about €4.5bn to interest expense (~15bp of GDP) against 119% debt/GDP and 0.4% growth; Le Pen's €140bn-by-2032 savings target implies a primary surplus France hasn't run since the early 2000s.

cards.claim: Citadel Securities argues the case for tighter policy remains compelling given fiscal largesse, resilient labour markets and an energy shock layered onto years of above-target inflation.
